prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Feel the patient’s heart Pounding—oh please, this once— —JAMES MERRILL I’ll do what I must if I’m bold in real time. A refugee, I’ll be paroled in real time. Cool evidence clawed off like shirts of hell-fire? A former existence untold in real time ... The one you would choose: Were you led then by him? What longing, O Yaar, is controlled in real time? Each syllable sucked under waves of our earth— The funeral love comes to hold in real time! They left him alive so that he could be lonely— The god of small things is not consoled in real time. Please afterwards empty my pockets of keys— It’s hell in the city of gold in real time. God’s angels again are—for Satan!—forlorn. Salvation was bought but sin sold in real time. And who is the terrorist, who the victim? We’ll know if the country is polled in real time. “Behind a door marked DANGER” are being unwound the prayers my friend had enscrolled in real time. The throat of the rearview and sliding down it the Street of Farewell’s now unrolled in real time. I heard the incessant dissolving of silk— I felt my heart growing so old in real time. Her heart must be ash where her body lies burned. What hope lets your hands rake the cold in real time? Now Friend, the Belovèd has stolen your words— Read slowly: The plot will unfold in real time. (for Daniel Hall)

outputs.L2:
Sense the sick person’s heart hammering—just this time, please.  
—JAMES MERRILL  

If courage holds in the present moment, I will fulfill my duty.  
Though displaced, I will receive release as events occur.  
Was cold proof torn away like clothing made of infernal flame?  
A previous life remains unspoken as time moves now...

The person you would select—was he the one who guided you then?  
O Yaar, what desire can be restrained in the immediate moment?  
Every sound is pulled beneath the surging ground of our world—  
Mourning love arrives to embrace us as it happens.

They spared his life only to leave him isolated.  
The deity concerned with little things finds no comfort in the present.  
Later, please remove every key from my pockets.  
Within the golden city, the here and now is torment.

Once more, God’s angels stand desolate—for Satan’s sake.  
Redemption was purchased, while wrongdoing was traded in the moment.  
Which person is the attacker, and which is the casualty?  
A live national survey may reveal the answer.

Beyond an entrance labeled “DANGER,”  
the prayers my friend once inscribed are now being unraveled.  
The rearview mirror forms a narrow passage, and slipping through it,  
the Avenue of Parting stretches open before us.

I listened to silk continually melting away.  
I sensed my heart aging in the very instant.  
Where her burned remains rest, her heart must have become cinders.  
What hope drives your fingers to comb through the cold right now?

And now, my Friend, the Belovèd has taken possession of your language.  
Take your time reading: the story will disclose itself as it happens.

*(for Daniel Hall)*
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker confronting exile, loneliness, and the demand to act courageously as a crisis unfolds. This personal struggle takes place within a world marked by violence, death, and mourning, where love and consolation remain present but seem increasingly fragile in the face of devastation. By asking who is labeled a terrorist and who is acknowledged as a victim, the poem challenges political categories and exposes how language can shape public perceptions of guilt, innocence, and suffering.

Religious imagery deepens this moral uncertainty. References to salvation, sin, angels, and evil suggest that traditional distinctions between good and bad have become entangled in a reality where judgment is difficult and certainty is suspect. At the same time, the speaker addresses a lost friend, giving the poem an intimate emotional center. Through this act of remembrance, the speaker reflects on aging, absence, and grief, recognizing that the meaning of traumatic events does not arrive all at once. Instead, it emerges gradually, even as history is still unfolding and those who survive struggle to understand what they have witnessed.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts exile, violence, grief, faith, and political uncertainty through a ghazal-like sequence whose recurring phrase “in real time” binds fragmented images and questions. Like the traditional ghazal, the poem moves through discrete yet emotionally connected moments rather than developing a single linear narrative. Each section offers another glimpse of displacement, suffering, memory, or doubt, while the refrain repeatedly returns the reader to the urgency of the present. “In real time” suggests that violence and loss are not safely contained in history or recollection; they continue to unfold as the poem is written, read, and understood.

This recurring phrase also complicates the relationship between witnessing and representation. Political catastrophe reaches the speaker through images, reports, memories, and personal associations, but the poem refuses to turn suffering into a coherent or easily interpreted story. Its fragmented structure reflects a world in which events occur too quickly and painfully to be fully processed. Questions remain unanswered, transitions are abrupt, and private grief merges with collective trauma. The speaker’s experience of exile is therefore both geographical and psychological: home survives as memory and longing, yet it remains altered or inaccessible.

Faith provides another language through which the poem approaches loss, but it does not supply simple certainty. Religious echoes, invocations, and questions suggest a desire for meaning in the face of violence, even as suffering tests the possibility of belief. The poem inhabits the tension between prayer and protest, consolation and accusation. Its spiritual dimension is not an escape from politics; instead, faith becomes another site where historical injustice and personal sorrow must be confronted.

The ghazal-like form is especially suited to these tensions. Because its units can stand partly on their own, the poem can place distant places, different forms of grief, and conflicting emotional states beside one another without forcing them into a single argument. At the same time, the repeated refrain creates continuity, making each fragment feel like part of one accumulating lament. Repetition does not resolve the speaker’s pain. Rather, it intensifies it, showing how grief returns and how political uncertainty enters every attempt to speak.

Ultimately, the poem presents personal and collective loss as immediate, unresolved, and inseparable. Individual sorrow becomes a way of apprehending public catastrophe, while public violence reshapes the speaker’s most intimate memories and beliefs. Poetry cannot reverse exile, restore the dead, or provide political certainty. It can, however, preserve names, images, questions, and emotional truths that might otherwise be erased. In this sense, the poem bears witness “in real time,” offering not closure but a fragile form of attention and solidarity. Its consolation lies in the act of speaking itself: incomplete and vulnerable, yet still capable of resisting silence.

JAMES could feel the pounding before he understood where it came from. At first, he thought it was his heart, beating wildly in the darkness. Then the walls began to tremble.

The sound grew louder—slow, heavy, relentless.

He reached for the door, but the handle turned before his fingers touched it. A cold wind swept into the room, carrying a whisper that seemed to come from everywhere at once.

“James.”

The pounding stopped.

For one breathless moment, there was only silence.

Then something knocked from inside the wall.
